title: Teaching students to play wrong notes and modes
summary: He has students practice outside notes on So What and discusses how modes are really used.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If you’re teaching a student and they are, let’s supposed they’re playing on “So What.” And they’re obviously missing the half-step change. My question is about wrong notes. What term do you use with them with — I mean wrong notes now seems to be a thing like well don’t call them wrong notes. So how do you approach them with — you’re playing wrong notes. That’s the best I can say.

Yeah what I do is I actually make students play wrong notes. I’ll do a tune like “So What” and I’ll just say okay, let’s figure out the notes that are going to sound bad on D minor seventh, okay? Let’s figure the notes that are going to be something, and let’s work on hitting that note. E flat. Right? Okay, and F sharp on the D minor seven chord. Let’s practice hitting those notes, first of all to get rid of the fear of hitting a wrong note. Because that’s one thing that keeps people from going, keeps them from searching, is they’re always afraid like oops I’m going to — so I just say, “Okay let’s play a blues.” I play a blues and I say, “Just play as much activity that you want that is chromatic and out but resolve it toward the end, come back into the chord.” So if you’ve got D minor seventh, play three bars out of chromatic nonsense no matter what you hear but get into the D minor back at the end. Now hold some of those notes that you find unpleasant and resolve them. See where they go, so that if you’re ever into that spot where — but don’t be afraid of them. Because those sometimes are the strengthening notes that pull you into the chord some — you know upper and lower — well I don’t want to get too technical, but upper and lower — appoggiatura — upper and lower chord tones, half step above, half step below, pentatonics. I do that all the time with the students. If I have them playing on a D minor pentatonic I’ll say, okay play the pentatonic a flat six away and a flat five — or you know a sharp five and a flat five away. So D minor right, with the B flat minor pentatonic, play a couple of notes of B flat minor, come into D minor. More notes of B flat minor, come back in. Do the same thing — it’s the root and the fifth, right? Because in harmony the fifth can always be replaced by another note. The root has to be there but the fifth is one of the notes that you can kind of get rid of on a chord and still keep the quality, right? So this is a device to train you. So D minor seventh, you would play E flat minor pentatonic, right, or a C sharp minor into D, right? Or a half step above the fifth, B flat minor or A flat minor below the fifth. But you just play a few of those notes and then come back in. And then a few notes out and then come back. Just get used to hearing those notes out but feel the resolution. That’s a little more advanced than learning how to play one or two wrong notes, but those are devices that you can use because if you hear anybody play “So What” nobody plays in the mode at all. Maybe Miles’ first solo he stayed pretty strict into the D minor, but then after that everybody

went out, in and out of the chord, up or low, the neighbor tones, there’s so many devices, with Trane it was superimposed “Giant Steps” changes over it before he would come back in. But there was so much theory there, but it all came from the fact that if you want to play the Dorian mode in a church setting the way those church modes, fine. You stay in the mode in a traditional way of speaking. But nobody ever plays that way when you’re playing.

That’s very interesting because we make such a big deal out of modes. But I’m not sure that the people that are making a big deal about it are actually players. Sometimes they are critics trying to figure out how to describe —

I mean what we learn as modes, I mean everybody’s been playing those for centuries and improvising on them too you know. It gets a little bit hairier if you go on to more advanced thinking like Messian, you know Messian the composer, his modes of limited transposition take you in another direction, they’re a whole different way of thinking about music. You know the altered scales and the diminished scales and all those things, the pentatonic scales and the Hungarian double harmonics and all of these scales — people use them in jazz but —
